timed_text.text: May 15th, you chose your focus anchor earlier in this program,
a word or phrase your mind returns to when it starts to drift.
Today I want to take that further,
because the most powerful version of an anchor
isn't just a word in your head.
It's something physical, something that exists
in the actual space where you compete.
Elite athletes do this instinctively,
a basketball player who bounces the ball exactly three times
before a free throw, a sprinter who locks eyes
on the same spot on the track before the gun.
A quarterback who taps his wrist band
before walking to the line,
these aren't superstitions.
They're trained to focus triggers,
physical anchors that pull the mind back
to the present moment on command.
The key is consistency.
The same thing the same way every single time,
because your nervous system responds to patterns.
When you perform that cue enough times in a focus state,
the cue begins to trigger the state.
That is conditioning.
That's what we're building today.
Think about the physical environment where you compete.
What is something you can see, touch, feel or do?
Something that is always available in that space
that you can turn into your competition anchor.
On your screen, you're gonna identify it and lock it in.

cards.prompt: Think about the physical space where you compete. What do you see, hear, or feel in that environment that is always there — every competition, every time?

Identify your physical anchor — something in that space, or something you wear or carry, that you can use as a consistent focus trigger. Something you can touch, see, or do deliberately before or during competition.
Design the moment — exactly when in competition will you use this anchor? Between plays? Before the starting signal? After a mistake? Write the specific moment and the exact action.
Say your focus word once. Feel your attention settle. That word plus that physical anchor — those two together are your return to center.

timed_text.text: Every time you use the physical anchor, you're strengthening the connection between that
action and your focus state.
Do it in practice, do it in warm-ups, do it in competition.
The more consistent you are, the faster it works when the pressure is real.
